summary: Akutagawa began attending Soseki's Thursday salon in late 1915 and became one of his disciples. In February 1916, after reading "The Nose," Soseki wrote him a letter saying that if he wrote another twenty-odd stories like it, he would have no equal in the literary world. This letter effectively decided Akutagawa's literary debut.

During his student years in Tokyo, Lu Xun drew on Nietzsche and Stirner in his classical-Chinese essay "On the Imbalanced Development of Culture" (文化偏至論), arguing for the individual spirit against the material civilization of the majority. He later also translated the preface of Thus Spoke Zarathustra into Chinese.

Lu Xun personally translated one of Soseki's stories for the Anthology of Modern Japanese Fiction (1923), which he compiled together with Zhou Zuoren, and in the author's note he introduced Chinese readers to Soseki's "leisure-school" (余裕派) detachment from plot events.

In the same Anthology of Modern Japanese Fiction (1923), Lu Xun translated Akutagawa's "The Nose" and "Rashomon" into Chinese. This was the channel through which Akutagawa's method of grafting modern motives onto the frame of classical tales reached Chinese readers in the early years of vernacular (baihua) fiction.

In 1936, Lu Xun translated eight of Chekhov's early humorous stories together as Bad Boy and Other Strange Tales (壞孩子和別的奇聞). This was an indirect translation based on a European-language edition rather than the Russian original, and it belongs to the final phase of the translation work he carried on into his last years.

In his 1923 lecture "What Happens After Nora Leaves Home," given at Beijing Women's Higher Normal School, Lu Xun took the ending of A Doll's House exactly as given and answered that awakening without economic means ends only in degradation or a return home. The remark revisited the New Culture Movement's reception of Ibsen from within.

Yeats wrote the introduction to the first edition of Song Offerings (1912), Tagore's own English translation, and introduced him to the London literary world; the following year's Nobel Prize in Literature came by way of that channel. This is recorded not as literary discipleship but as editorial patronage that mediated Tagore's entry into the English-speaking world.

Nim ui Chimmuk (1926) includes the poem "On Reading Tagore's Poems (GARDENISTO)," so the bare fact that Han Yong-un read Tagore survives within the collection itself. However, explaining the vocative address of this honorific-register prose poem and the figure of "the Beloved (nim)" as products of Tagore's reception is a lineage that Korean modern-poetry scholarship has repeatedly drawn; because the channel passed through Korean-language translation, it is not treated here as direct influence.

Histories of modern Korean poetry place Azaleas (1925) and Nim ui Chimmuk (1926) side by side as two answers to the same question — in what voice should one call out to the beloved who has left. Kim Sowol answered with the three-beat meter of folk song and a resigned speaker; Han Yong-un answered with an honorific-register prose poem carrying Buddhist paradox.

Trilce (1922) and "Crow's Eye View" (1934) each broke the orthographic conventions of Spanish and Korean on the printed page. There is no record of direct contact or mutual awareness between the two poets. This map places them side by side as two cases in which peripheral poetry, instead of importing forms from the center, took the orthography of its own language as its material.

Premchand translated Tolstoy's short stories into Hindi and collected them as Tolstoy's Stories (1923). This work of transposing the structure of moral fables into cases from rural India belongs to a stage before the later Premchand, who would strip moral judgment out of his narration.

The 1936 Polish edition of The Trial was published under Schulz's name, with an afterword by him. Since there is discussion over who actually did the translating, what is recorded here is only the fact that the edition appeared under his name with an afterword he wrote. It is the edition that established Kafka in the Polish-speaking world.

In 1936, the two exchanged open letters in the pages of the magazine Studio. Gombrowicz provoked Schulz by invoking the verdict of "the doctor's wife from Wilcza Street" and claiming that Schulz's art leaned on the authority of form, and Schulz answered in kind; this exchange records two lines of interwar Polish prose colliding directly. Schulz later also wrote a critical essay on Ferdydurke.

From 1939, Gombrowicz spent twenty-four years in Buenos Aires, where his Diary repeatedly attacked Borges and the Europe-facing culture of the Sur group, and the Spanish translation of Ferdydurke was produced collaboratively in cafés outside that literary establishment. Argentine-Polish comparative literature has repeatedly taken up a reading that opposes the two along two terms: the library as a completed form, and the unfinishedness of immaturity.

Pirandello's masks and Gombrowicz's "face" (gęba) both turn the form one is forced to put on before others into the very action of the drama. No record has been found confirming contact or influence between the two. This map places them side by side as two cases that independently built the same device.

In 1936 in Vienna, Canetti gave the speech for Broch's fiftieth birthday, addressing his conception of the novel head-on, and his autobiography The Play of the Eyes records the conversations the two exchanged across several chapters. It was also Broch who brought Canetti into the Vienna literary world.

In the lecture "James Joyce and the Present Age," written for Joyce's fiftieth birthday, Broch read Ulysses as a novelistic form capable of bearing the totality of consciousness, and that reading carries through into the long interior-monologue construction of The Death of Virgil. When Broch was seized by the Nazi authorities in 1938, Joyce was among those who helped him leave the country.

The Man Without Qualities (1930) and The Sleepwalkers (1931–32) were written in Vienna in the same period, sharing the same project of narrating the collapse of a value system by admitting essayistic argument into the novel. German-language scholarship treats the two works side by side as two forms of the "essayistic novel."

The essayistic chapter "The Disintegration of Values," inserted into The Sleepwalkers, brings into the novel the diagnosis that once God is dead, the value system splinters into mutually unrelated partial logics. Broch scholarship locates the starting point of this diagnosis in the problem of nihilism after Nietzsche.

In The Play of the Eyes, Canetti recorded Musil's reaction to reading Auto-da-Fé. Musil first praised the novel, then withdrew his approval on hearing that Broch had given it the same praise, and Canetti described that moment of retraction as an illustration of how hierarchy operated in the Vienna literary world.

In 1931, Canetti sent the manuscript of Auto-da-Fé to Thomas Mann, who returned it unread. After the book was published in 1935, Mann read it and sent a letter of praise, and in The Play of the Eyes Canetti recorded these two letters as the two phases of his entry into the literary world.

In The Torch in My Ear, Canetti recorded meeting Brecht in Berlin in 1928. Canetti, twenty-three years old and insisting on the seriousness of literature, was met with Brecht's cynicism, and he described this encounter as the moment his own view of literature was fixed.

After reading the whole of Kafka's letters to Felice Bauer, Canetti wrote the book Kafka's Other Trial (1969). Reading this correspondence of engagement and broken engagement as a document of power relations, the work applies the method of Crowds and Power to one writer's private life.

In 1926, Rilke and Tsvetaeva exchanged a three-way correspondence, mediated by Pasternak, that lasted a little over half a year. That summer Rilke wrote an "Elegy" dedicated to her, and when Rilke died that December, Tsvetaeva answered with "New Year's Greeting." The two never met in person.

In 1916, Tsvetaeva wrote the cycle "To Akhmatova," and Akhmatova later answered with a poem dedicated to her, "A Belated Reply." The two women actually met only once, for two days in Moscow in June 1941, and on that occasion Akhmatova read Poem Without a Hero aloud to her.

In 1940, after returning to the Soviet Union and relying on translation for her living, Tsvetaeva translated the final poem of The Flowers of Evil, "Le Voyage," into Russian as "Плаванье" (Plavanye). This translation, which preserved the original's rhyme structure, became the Baudelaire version most repeatedly quoted in the Russian-speaking world.

Among the last work Tsvetaeva undertook after returning to the Soviet Union in 1939 was a Russian translation of Lorca's poems. Cut short by her death in 1941, this translation belongs on the path by which Lorca was introduced into Soviet print after the Spanish Civil War.

During the period when publication of her own poetry was blocked, Akhmatova made her living through translation, and Tagore's poems were among the works on that list. Since she did not know Bengali, she used a literal translation as her base text — exactly the method the Soviet translation system assigned to its poets.

Hedayat translated Kafka into Persian, and in the long introduction "Kafka's Message," attached to the 1948 Persian edition of In the Penal Colony, he gave Iranian readers their first systematic introduction to Kafka. Because there is disagreement over who is credited as translator for individual works, what is recorded here is this introduction and the introductory work he led.

Tagore's 1924 lectures in China were read as a defense of Eastern spiritual civilization, and the New Culture Movement camp rejected this outright. In his 1934 essay "Kill by Cursing, Kill by Praising," Lu Xun targeted the segment of the Chinese literary world that had enshrined Tagore like a living immortal. This is the point where two starting points of colonial and semi-colonial Asia diverged over tradition.

Histories of modern Indian literature place the two writers as two directions within the same period. Tagore moved into the international literary world through Bengali lyric poetry and self-translation, while Premchand turned the material of Hindi-Urdu prose into rent and debt. Premchand's 1936 presidential address to the Progressive Writers' Association, defining literature as a measure of reality rather than entertainment, is the document of that choice of direction.

The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas (1881) and I Am a Cat (1905) both take up the imported form of the European novel and answer it with a digressive first-person narrator and irony. There is no record of contact or reading between the two writers. This map places them side by side as two ways in which peripheral fiction handles the norms of the center.

Both men held technical posts in government offices, writing between an institutional language that was not their own and their own language. Kafka wrote in the German of Prague; Yi Sang published in Gyeongseong, moving between Japanese and Korean. There is no record that Yi Sang read Kafka. This map groups them under the condition of minority-language prose written from inside an institution.
